description.sr_latin: Fraze za jutarnje rutine, kućne poslove, večernje opuštanje i zajednički život.
description.en: Phrases for morning routines, household chores, evening chill time, and living together.

phrases.context: Waking up your partner or friend who's oversleeping.
phrases.notes: 'Ustaj' is the imperative of 'ustati' (to get up). Casual and direct.

phrases.context: The universal reply when someone tries to wake you up.
phrases.notes: 'Još' means 'more/still'. You'll hear this constantly.

phrases.context: Offering to make coffee in the morning. This is practically a love language in Serbia.
phrases.notes: 'Kafa' (from Turkish) is sacred — domaća, Turkish-style coffee, not espresso. Croatians say 'kava', Bosnians 'kahva'.

phrases.context: Asking your partner to make coffee. Add 'molim te' to keep it sweet.
phrases.notes: 'Napravi' = imperative of 'napraviti' (to make). Works for food/drinks.

phrases.en: Who's going to the bathroom first?
phrases.context: The daily negotiation when you share one bathroom.
phrases.notes: 'Kupatilo' = bathroom. In Bosnia you might also hear 'kupaonica'.

phrases.context: When your partner is taking forever in the bathroom.
phrases.notes: 'Požuri' = hurry (imperative). 'Kasnim' = I'm late (from 'kasniti').

phrases.context: Casual morning conversation about outfits.
phrases.notes: 'Oblačiti' = to put on (clothes). Present tense used for 'going to wear'.

phrases.context: Asking what's available to eat in the morning.
phrases.notes: 'Doručak' = breakfast. 'Ručak' = lunch. 'Večera' = dinner.

phrases.context: You shuffle into the kitchen first thing and there's nothing out yet — groan how ravenous you are.
phrases.notes: If you're female, say 'Gladna sam kao vuk.' Adjective changes gender.

phrases.en: I cook, you wash the dishes.
phrases.context: Dividing kitchen duties fairly (or trying to).
phrases.notes: 'Kuhati' = to cook (in Serbia you'll more often hear 'kuvati / kuvam' — the v/h swap is a classic Serbian vs Bosnian/Croatian tell). 'Prati sudove' = to wash dishes.

phrases.context: The eternal household debate.
phrases.notes: 'Prati/perati sudove' = to wash dishes. 'Sudovi' = dishes (plural).

phrases.context: Suggesting it's time to clean up.
phrases.notes: 'Treba da' + present tense = 'need to'. Very common construction. 'Usisati' = to vacuum.

phrases.context: Asking someone to take the garbage out.
phrases.notes: 'Đubre' = trash/garbage (a Turkish loanword, originally 'manure'). 'Izneti' = to take out.

phrases.sr_latin: Veš neće sam sebe da opere.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Веш неће сам себе да опере.
phrases.context: A passive-aggressive nudge to get someone to do laundry.
phrases.notes: 'Veš' = laundry. This sarcastic phrasing is very natural in Serbian.

phraseGroups.theme: Asking Your Partner to Do Something

phrases.sr_latin: Možeš li da odeš do prodavnice?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Можеш ли да одеш до продавнице?
phrases.en: Can you go to the store?
phrases.context: Asking your partner to run an errand.
phrases.notes: 'Možeš li da...' = 'Can you...' Polite but casual way to ask for something.

phrases.context: Asking for a hand with something around the house.
phrases.notes: 'Pomozi' = help (imperative of 'pomoći'). 'Malo' softens the request.

phrases.sr_latin: Može da skuvaš nešto za večeru?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Може да скуваш нешто за вечеру?
phrases.en: Could you cook something for dinner?
phrases.context: Gently asking your partner to handle dinner.
phrases.notes: 'Može da...' is a softer, more colloquial way to ask than 'Možeš li da...'

phrases.context: Suggesting you watch a show or movie together in the evening.
phrases.notes: 'Ajde da...' = 'Let's...' — one of the most useful constructions in casual Serbian.

phrases.en: What do you want to watch?
phrases.context: Letting the other person pick what to watch.
phrases.notes: 'Šta ćeš da...' = 'What will you / what do you want to...'

phrases.sr_latin: Umoran sam, ceo dan sam radio.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Уморан сам, цео дан сам радио.
phrases.en: I'm tired, I worked all day.
phrases.context: Explaining why you just want to crash on the couch.
phrases.notes: Feminine: 'Umorna sam, ceo dan sam radila.' Adjective and past tense change.

variations.sr_latin: Umorna sam, ceo dan sam radila.
variations.sr_cyrillic: Уморна сам, цео дан сам радила.
variations.en: I'm tired, I worked all day.

phrases.context: The classic couch battle.
phrases.notes: 'Daljinski' = remote control (short for 'daljinski upravljač').

phrases.context: Suggesting it's time for bed.
phrases.notes: 'Spavati' = to sleep. 'Ajde da spavamo' is the natural way to say 'let's go to bed'.

phrases.context: You're turning in for the night and say the plain bedtime line that works with anyone.
Asking someone to kill the lights before sleep.
phrases.notes: 'Ugasiti' = to turn off / extinguish. Also used for TV, phone, etc.

phrases.context: When you're tossing and turning at night.
phrases.notes: 'Ne mogu da...' = 'I can't...' Very common pattern.

phrases.context: The daily panic before leaving the house.
phrases.notes: 'Ključevi' = keys (plural of 'ključ').

phrases.context: Reminding someone to lock up when leaving or before bed.
phrases.notes: 'Vrata' is neuter plural — always plural in Serbian, even for one door.

phrases.context: Texting your partner or asking when they'll be back.
phrases.notes: 'Kući' = home (dative, used for direction). 'Kod kuće' = at home.

phrases.context: Letting someone know you need to restock something.
phrases.notes: 'Ponestati' = to run out of. Swap 'mleka' for whatever's gone — 'hleba' (bread), 'kafe' (coffee). In Bosnia it's 'mlijeko' (and 'hljeb').

phrases.context: Declaring a full lazy day at home.
phrases.notes: 'Nigde' = nowhere. Double negatives are standard and required in Serbian.

phrases.context: The lazy Sunday lifestyle declaration.
phrases.notes: 'Pidžama' = pajamas. 'Ceo dan' = all day.

phrases.context: Suggesting you order food delivery instead of cooking.
phrases.notes: 'Naručiti' = to order. Works for food delivery, in a restaurant, online shopping.

phrases.sr_latin: Ma hajde da ležimo ceo dan.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Ма хајде да лежимо цео дан.
phrases.en: Let's just lie around all day.
phrases.context: Peak lazy Sunday energy. No plans, no obligations.
phrases.notes: 'Ma' at the start adds a dismissive/carefree tone, like 'oh just' or 'come on'.

phrases.context: Asking your partner about their day when you reconnect in the evening.
phrases.notes: 'Dan' is masculine, so 'bio' (m. past participle). Natural and warm.

phrases.context: Casual follow-up about someone's day.
phrases.notes: Feminine form: 'Šta si radila danas?'

phrases.sr_latin: Baš sam se smorio na poslu.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Баш сам се сморио на послу.
phrases.en: I was so bored at work.
phrases.context: Complaining about a boring day at work.
phrases.notes: 'Smoriti se' = to get bored/fed up. Very colloquial. Feminine: 'smorila'.

variations.sr_latin: Baš sam se smorila na poslu.
variations.sr_cyrillic: Баш сам се сморила на послу.
variations.en: I was so bored at work.
